config.editorData:
vSAN overview — which layer is broken?

The pager went off and you do not yet know where to look. Each table below is a layer of the IO path, top to bottom, and the job of this screen is to point at one of them inside a minute. Then move to the matching detail screen.

Normal is front end above back end. The front end carries network hops, owner coordination and policy work the disks never see, so it should read higher. The two converging, or inverting, is the anomaly — not either number on its own.

The owner row between them is new. It is the layer that coordinates each write across its replicas, so it holds the cost of making a write durable in more than one place. When the front end is slow and the back end is not, the owner row is usually where the difference went.

Capacity

Renders the vSAN Cluster Capacity view.

Free Capacity — Unused vSAN capacity. Read it next to Total, not alone: the same free figure means very different things on a 10 TB and a 1 PB cluster.

Used Capacity — Consumed vSAN capacity, after deduplication and compression.

Total Capacity — Usable vSAN capacity. Already excludes the overhead vSAN reserves for itself, so it is smaller than the sum of the disks.

Space Efficiency Ratio — Space saving from deduplication and compression, expressed as a ratio scaled by 100 -- 134 means 1.34:1, not 134:1. A ratio that falls sharply usually means new data that does not deduplicate, not a fault.

Saved Capacity — Bytes not written because deduplication and compression removed them. The absolute saving behind the ratio beside it.

Front end - what VMs feel

Renders the vSAN Cluster DOM Client view.

Read Latency — Average read latency at this layer. Compare the same column across the client, owner and component manager views: the layer where the number first becomes large is the layer to investigate.

Write Latency — Average write latency at this layer. On ESA a write is acknowledged after it is logged, so this is usually far lower than the component manager's figure beneath it.

Congestions — vSAN's own backpressure signal, raised when a layer cannot absorb the offered load and asks the layer above to slow down. Zero on a healthy cluster, and it reads zero here. Any sustained non-zero value is the single most important number on the screen.

Read Congestions — Backpressure attributed to reads.

Write Congestions — Backpressure attributed to writes.

Unmap congestion — Backpressure attributed to unmap and space-reclamation work.

Read IOPS — Read operations per second. Always read beside latency: high latency at high IOPS is a busy VM, high latency at near-zero IOPS is a sick one.

Write IOPS — Write operations per second.

Outstanding IO — Outstanding IO: operations issued and not yet completed. Latency multiplied by nothing tells you why it is high -- this does. High latency with high outstanding IO is queueing, high latency with low outstanding IO is a slow device.

Read Throughput — Bytes per second read at this layer.

Write Throughput — Bytes per second written at this layer.

Coordination - the owner

Renders the vSAN Cluster DOM Owner view.

Read Latency — Average read latency at this layer. Compare the same column across the client, owner and component manager views: the layer where the number first becomes large is the layer to investigate.

Write Latency — Average write latency at this layer. On ESA a write is acknowledged after it is logged, so this is usually far lower than the component manager's figure beneath it.

Read IOPS — Read operations per second. Always read beside latency: high latency at high IOPS is a busy VM, high latency at near-zero IOPS is a sick one.

Write IOPS — Write operations per second.

Read Throughput — Bytes per second read. The owner layer names its throughput columns differently from the client layer; the quantity is the same.

Write Throughput — Bytes per second written.

Outstanding IO — Outstanding IO: operations issued and not yet completed. Latency multiplied by nothing tells you why it is high -- this does. High latency with high outstanding IO is queueing, high latency with low outstanding IO is a slow device.

Congestions — vSAN's own backpressure signal, raised when a layer cannot absorb the offered load and asks the layer above to slow down. Zero on a healthy cluster, and it reads zero here. Any sustained non-zero value is the single most important number on the screen.

Read Congestions — Backpressure attributed to reads.

Write Congestions — Backpressure attributed to writes.

Back end - the disks

Renders the vSAN Cluster DOM Component Manager view.

Read Latency — Average read latency at this layer. Compare the same column across the client, owner and component manager views: the layer where the number first becomes large is the layer to investigate.

Write Latency — Average write latency at this layer. On ESA a write is acknowledged after it is logged, so this is usually far lower than the component manager's figure beneath it.

Congestions — vSAN's own backpressure signal, raised when a layer cannot absorb the offered load and asks the layer above to slow down. Zero on a healthy cluster, and it reads zero here. Any sustained non-zero value is the single most important number on the screen.

Outstanding IO — Outstanding IO: operations issued and not yet completed. Latency multiplied by nothing tells you why it is high -- this does. High latency with high outstanding IO is queueing, high latency with low outstanding IO is a slow device.

Read IOPS — Read operations per second. Always read beside latency: high latency at high IOPS is a busy VM, high latency at near-zero IOPS is a sick one.

Write IOPS — Write operations per second.

Transport - RDT

Renders the vSAN Cluster RDT view.

RDT Network Cluster Average Latency — Average round-trip latency of vSAN's own transport between hosts. This sits above TCP, so it can be slow while every NIC counter is clean.

RDT Network Cluster Max Latency — Worst round-trip latency observed. Spikes here matter more than the average -- one stalled transfer blocks whatever was waiting on it.

RDT Network Cluster Min Latency — Best round-trip latency observed. Useful only as a floor to compare the average against.

RDT Network Average Outbound Queueing Latency — Average time a message waited in the outbound queue before being sent. Queueing, as opposed to time on the wire.

RDT Network Socket Min Outbound Bytes (Low Is Bad) — Lowest free space seen in the outbound socket buffer. Low is bad -- this measures headroom remaining, so it reads backwards from every other column. Zero means exhaustion and a stalled transport.

RDT Network Socket Min Inbound Bytes (Low Is Bad) — Lowest free space seen in the inbound socket buffer. Low is bad, for the same reason.

Keepalive reset (Total) — Lifetime count of keepalive resets: RDT gave up on a peer connection and re-established it. Cumulative since boot, so the number itself means little -- watch whether it is increasing.

Num ready delay (Total) — Lifetime count of delays waiting for a connection to become ready. Cumulative since boot; the trend is the signal.

Host health and load

Renders the vSphere Host Uplinks and Load view.

Uplink RX Errors, All NICs — Inbound errors summed across every uplink on the host, counted by vCenter rather than by this pack. This pack only measures uplinks that carry vSAN traffic, which on this cluster is two of four per host, so a standby uplink going bad is invisible to it. This column is here to close that gap.

Uplink RX Dropped, All NICs — Inbound packets dropped across every uplink on the host.

Uplink TX Errors, All NICs — Outbound errors across every uplink on the host.

Uplink TX Dropped, All NICs — Outbound packets dropped across every uplink on the host.

Host Network Throughput — Total host network throughput, all uplinks and all traffic types. Context for the error columns and a check on whether vSAN is a large or a small share of what this host is doing.

Host CPU Usage — Host CPU usage from vCenter. On the screen so that vSAN latency can be read against host load: a saturated host produces vSAN latency that is not a vSAN problem.

Host CPU Contention — Proportion of time virtual machines waited for CPU. This, not usage, is the contention signal -- a host can be busy without anything waiting, and can make things wait while looking only moderately busy.

Host Memory Consumed — Proportion of host memory consumed.

Host Memory Swap-In Rate — Rate at which the host is reading memory back from disk. Any sustained non-zero value is serious: it means memory was overcommitted far enough to page, and every latency figure on every other panel becomes unreliable while it continues.

Host Uptime — Host uptime. Relevant here because many counters in this pack are cumulative since boot, so a recently rebooted host has small totals for reasons that have nothing to do with health.

Hardware Sensor Status — Overall hardware sensor health, as the host's own sensors report it. This replaced a set of vSAN daemon liveness columns that could not be displayed: those carry a current value but no retained history, and a view queries a time range, so every cell came back blank.

Connectivity Issues, Critical — Count of critical connectivity findings against this host. A tripwire rather than a diagnosis -- it tells you something is wrong and not what.

Utilisation Issues, Critical — Count of critical utilisation findings against this host.
